title: What God Actually Asks For
overview: The LORD brings a formal complaint against his people, reminds them of his past kindness, says plainly that he wants justice, kindness and humility rather than lavish offerings, and condemns the cheating and violence in Jerusalem.

parts.label: God takes Israel to court (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The scene is set like a court case, with the mountains and the ancient foundations of the earth called to listen as the LORD brings a formal complaint against his own people. Calling on the mountains makes the charge solemn and public, and one older reading adds that even rocks are asked to hear because the people themselves will not.

parts.label: What have I done to you? (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: God asks what he ever did to wear them out, then lists what he did for them: freeing them from slavery in Egypt, giving them Moses, Aaron and Miriam as leaders, and turning the curse that Balak king of Moab wanted from the prophet Balaam into a blessing. Shittim was their last camp before crossing the Jordan and Gilgal their first camp in the new land, so the phrase recalls God bringing them safely in.

parts.label: What does the LORD want? (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: A worshipper asks what offering would fix things, moving from costly young calves to impossible amounts of animals and oil, and even to sacrificing a firstborn child, a practice known in the region and condemned in Israel's law. The answer is that God has already made it clear: treat people fairly, love kindness and loyalty, and live humbly with God.

parts.label: Cheating in the city (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The LORD calls out to Jerusalem and tells them to take seriously the punishment, pictured as a rod, that he has appointed. Merchants were using undersized measures and rigged scales, the rich were violent, and lying was common (the middle line of verse 9 is unclear in the Hebrew, so translations differ).

parts.label: Effort that comes to nothing (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: The punishment echoes warnings in Israel's law: they will eat but stay hungry, save but lose it, plant but never harvest, press olives and grapes but never enjoy the oil or wine. The picture fits the wrongdoing, since wealth gained by cheating will not last.

parts.label: Copying Omri and Ahab (v. 16)
parts.note: Omri and his son Ahab were kings of the northern kingdom, remembered in the Bible as among its worst rulers, especially for promoting the worship of other gods. Judah has followed their ways, so it will face ruin and become something other nations mock.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 8 sums up everything God asks of people, or sets a standard no one fully meets that points to the need for grace.
think: When people try to make things right after doing wrong, why might a big gesture feel easier than changing how they treat others day to day?
